title: Repairing school uniforms
paragraphs: At Eastfield School, a pile of unwanted uniforms used to appear at the end of every academic year. Some items were too small, some had minor damage and others were simply no longer needed. A parent group argued that sending usable clothing to textile recycling should be the last step, not the first.

The school created a repair-and-exchange programme. Volunteers replace buttons, repair loose seams and remove old name labels. Families can donate uniforms anonymously and take another item without proving financial need. Organizers say this matters because a scheme presented only as charity may discourage families who would otherwise use it.

The programme has environmental limits. Not every item can be repaired, and some synthetic fabrics are difficult to recycle when they are finally worn out. The organizers therefore want the school to consider durability when choosing future suppliers. A cheaper shirt that lasts one year may create more waste and cost families more over time than a stronger one that lasts several years.

After one year, the school estimates that hundreds of items have remained in use longer. The organizers are careful not to claim that clothing exchange solves the environmental impact of uniforms. Their wider goal is to change the sequence of decisions: use, repair, share and only then recycle or replace.

questions.prompt: What problem did the parent group identify?
options: Students had no uniforms at all.
Usable uniforms were being discarded or recycled before reuse options were considered.
The school had too many repair volunteers.
Uniforms were made only from natural fabrics.
questions.explanationJa: usable clothingをすぐrecycleするのではなくreuseを優先すべきと考えました。

questions.prompt: Give two things volunteers do to prepare donated uniforms for reuse.
markscheme: They replace buttons and/or repair loose seams.
questions.explanationJa: minor repairsとname-label removalです。

questions.prompt: True or false: Families must prove financial need before taking a uniform.
questions.justification: Families can donate and take items anonymously without proving financial need.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。stigmaを避けるためmeans testはありません。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 3 meaning 'the ability to last for a long time without becoming damaged'.
questions.explanationJa: durability＝耐久性。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 2, what does 'this' in 'Organizers say this matters' refer to?
options: Allowing families to use the exchange without proving financial need
Buying only new uniforms
Removing all school rules
Recycling every shirt immediately
questions.explanationJa: anonymous/open access designを指します。

questions.prompt: Why do organizers want durability considered when selecting suppliers? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Longer-lasting clothes can reduce waste because they need replacement less often.
A durable item may cost families less over time even if its initial price is higher.
questions.explanationJa: environmental wasteとlong-term costの両方です。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: The preferred sequence ends with recycle or ________.
questions.explanationJa: recycle or replace が最後です。

questions.prompt: What is the organizers' attitude toward the programme's success?
options: They claim it solves every environmental problem.
They value the results but see the programme as one part of a wider change in consumption decisions.
They want to end repairs immediately.
They believe recycling should always happen first.
questions.explanationJa: 成果を認めつつoverclaimせず、decision sequenceの変化を重視します。

questions.prompt: What two broader principles does the programme illustrate?
markscheme: Extending product life through repair and reuse can be preferable to immediate recycling or replacement.
Reuse systems work better when they are socially accessible and designed to avoid stigma.
questions.explanationJa: circular useとinclusive accessが中心です。

title: Who gets the garden water?
paragraphs: A community garden in a dry part of California faced conflict after water restrictions were introduced. Gardeners had previously watered plots whenever they wished, but the new monthly limit meant that one person's choices could reduce the amount available to everyone else.

The garden committee first considered giving every plot exactly the same allowance. Some members argued this was fair, while others pointed out that plots differed in size and purpose. A small herb bed required far less water than a plot growing vegetables for a community kitchen.

The final system combines a basic allowance with additional water for plots that meet agreed criteria, such as food donation or newly planted fruit trees. The garden also installed shared mulch and drip-irrigation equipment to reduce evaporation. Members must record water use, not to punish individuals, but to identify where the system is inefficient.

The committee says the policy is still an experiment. If gardeners focus only on protecting their own allocation, cooperation may weaken. The long-term goal is not to calculate the perfect number of litres for every person but to create rules that make scarcity visible and encourage members to solve the problem together.

questions.prompt: Why did water restrictions create a collective problem?
options: Every gardener had unlimited water.
Water used by one person could reduce what remained for others.
The garden stopped growing plants.
Rainfall increased dramatically.
questions.explanationJa: shared limited resourceなのでindividual choiceがothersに影響します。

questions.prompt: Why was an identical allowance for every plot questioned? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Plots were different sizes and therefore did not have equal water needs.
Plots served different purposes, including some growing food for community donation.
questions.explanationJa: sizeとpurposeが異なるためです。

questions.prompt: True or false: Extra water is given only to the largest plots.
questions.justification: Additional water is linked to agreed criteria such as food donation or newly planted fruit trees, not simply plot size.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。criteria-based allocationです。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 4 meaning 'a situation in which there is not enough of something'.
questions.explanationJa: scarcity＝不足・希少性。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, what does 'the system' refer to?
options: The garden's water-allocation and conservation system
The local school timetable
A vegetable market
A rainfall forecast
questions.explanationJa: water allocation/conservation system全体です。

questions.prompt: Give two ways the garden tries to reduce waste as well as allocate water.
markscheme: It uses shared mulch to reduce evaporation.
It uses drip irrigation and/or records use to identify inefficient areas.
questions.explanationJa: mulch、drip irrigation、monitoringです。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: The rules should make scarcity ________.
questions.explanationJa: make scarcity visible が本文です。

questions.prompt: What concern does the committee express about individual allocations?
options: People may focus only on protecting their own share and weaken cooperation.
Gardeners may use too little technology.
Every plot will become identical.
Food donations will automatically stop.
questions.explanationJa: individual entitlementだけに注目するとcooperationが弱くなる可能性があります。

questions.prompt: What idea of fairness does the report present? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Fairness does not necessarily mean identical amounts when needs and social purposes differ.
Fair rules should also encourage shared responsibility for conserving a limited resource, not only divide it among individuals.
questions.explanationJa: equal amountではなくneedとcollective responsibilityを含むfairnessです。

title: Night lights and invisible neighbours
paragraphs: A small coastal town has begun replacing some bright white streetlights with warmer, shielded lamps after researchers found unusually low numbers of night-flying insects near heavily lit roads. The change is not intended to make streets dark. Instead, planners want light to reach the ground where people need it rather than spreading upward and sideways.

Artificial light can affect insects in several ways. Some species circle lamps until they become exhausted, while others change feeding or mating behaviour. Because insects are food for birds and bats and also pollinate plants, changes at night can influence species that residents notice during the day.

The project has raised safety concerns. Some residents initially assumed that reducing light pollution meant reducing visibility. Engineers responded by measuring illumination on pavements before and after new lamps were installed. In several locations, shielded lights produced less glare while keeping walking surfaces equally visible because more of the light was directed downward.

Researchers caution that lighting is only one pressure on insect populations; pesticide use, habitat loss and climate also matter. They therefore describe the project as a targeted intervention rather than a complete solution. Its value will be judged through insect monitoring, energy use, resident surveys and safety data over several years.

questions.prompt: What is the main goal of the new streetlights?
options: To remove all street lighting
To direct necessary light more carefully and reduce unnecessary light pollution
To make roads brighter in every direction
To attract more insects to lamps
questions.explanationJa: needed illuminationは維持しつつspill lightを減らします。

questions.prompt: Give two ways artificial light can affect insects.
markscheme: Some insects circle lights until exhausted.
Light can alter feeding and/or mating behaviour.
questions.explanationJa: exhaustionとbehaviour changeです。

questions.prompt: True or false: Engineers responded to safety concerns only by asking residents for opinions.
questions.justification: They measured pavement illumination before and after installation and compared visibility as well as glare.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。objective illumination measurementも使っています。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 3 meaning 'uncomfortably strong brightness that makes it harder to see'.
questions.explanationJa: glare＝まぶしさ。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 4, what does 'the project' refer to?
options: The replacement of some streetlights with warmer shielded lamps
A pesticide campaign
A bird-counting competition
A coastal road expansion
questions.explanationJa: streetlight replacement projectです。

questions.prompt: Why can insect changes affect other species? Give two linked ideas.
markscheme: Insects provide food for animals such as birds and bats.
They also pollinate plants, so reduced insect activity can affect wider ecological relationships.
questions.explanationJa: food-web roleとpollination roleです。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: Researchers call the project a targeted ________.
questions.explanationJa: targeted intervention が本文です。

questions.prompt: What did engineers find about shielded lights in several locations?
options: They always reduced pavement visibility.
They reduced glare while maintaining similar visibility on walking surfaces.
They increased upward light.
They used more energy because light was less focused.
questions.explanationJa: less glareでもground visibilityは維持できました。

questions.prompt: Why will the project use several kinds of evidence over multiple years? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Insect monitoring and energy data can show environmental or efficiency effects.
Resident surveys and safety data can show whether the lighting change remains acceptable and safe for people.
questions.explanationJa: ecological outcomeとhuman/safety outcomeの両方を見ます。

questions.prompt: What is the writer's overall attitude toward the lighting project?
options: It is presented as a complete solution to insect decline.
It is a promising targeted measure whose effects should be tested alongside other pressures.
It is rejected because safety cannot be measured.
It matters only for energy bills.
questions.explanationJa: promising but limited interventionとしてbalancedに扱っています。
